Consider the vectors $$ \vvec_1 = \twovec{2}{1}, \vvec_2 = \twovec{1}{2} $$ in $\real^2$, which are shown in [fig-basis-1].

Linear combinations of $\vvec_1$ and $\vvec_2$.

Indicate the linear combination $\vvec_1 - 2\vvec_2$ on the figure.

We can see graphically, or we can compute, that $\vvec_1-2\vvec_2 = \twovec{0}{-3}$.

Express the vector $\twovec{-3}{0}$ as a linear combination of $\vvec_1$ and $\vvec_2$.

Again, we graphically see that $\twovec{-3}{0} = -2\vvec_1+\vvec_2$.

Find the linear combination $10\vvec_1 - 13\vvec_2$.

Since the linear combination extends beyond the figure, we compute that $10\vvec_1-13\vvec_2 = \twovec{7}{-16}$.

Express the vector $\twovec{16}{-4}$ as a linear combination of $\vvec_1$ and $\vvec_2$.

We need to find the solution to the linear system $c_1\vvec_1 + c_2\vvec_2 = \twovec{16}{-4}$, which is $\twovec{c_1}{c_2} = \twovec{12}{-8}$.

Explain why every vector in $\real^2$ can be written as a linear combination of $\vvec_1$ and $\vvec_2$ in exactly one way.

The matrix $\left[\begin{array}{rr} \vvec_1 \amp \vvec_2 \end{array}\right]$ has a pivot position in every row and every column.
